title: Alpha Cognition to Participate in Panel Discussion at the B. Riley Securities Mind, Muscle & Vision Summit
summary: Alpha Cognition Inc. brings excitement and passion to our work with the goal of positively impact the lives of people living with Alzheimer’s and ALS.
body_text: Alpha Cognition to Participate in Panel Discussion at the B. Riley Securities Mind, Muscle & Vision Summit VANCOUVER, British Columbia and Dallas, TX – July 10, 2026 - Alpha Cognition Inc. (Nasdaq: ACOG) (“Alpha Cognition”, or the “Company”), a biopharmaceutical company focused on developing novel therapies for debilitating neurodegenerative disorders, today announced Michael McFadden, Chief Executive Officer, will participate in the Late-Stage & Commercial CNS Small Cap panel discussion during the upcoming B. Riley Securities Mind, Muscle & Vision Summit, taking place July 16th in Boston, Massachusetts. The panel discussion will be held from 3:10 p.m. to 3:50 p.m. ET. For further information regarding this event or to schedule a 1x1 meeting during the summit, please reach out to your institutional representative at B. Riley. There will be no live webcast of the panel discussion. About Alpha Cognition Inc. Alpha Cognition Inc. is a commercial stage, biopharmaceutical company dedicated to developing treatments for patients suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease and Cognitive Impairment with mild Traumatic Brain Injury (“mTBI”), for which there are currently no approved treatment options. ZUNVEYL is a patented acetylcholinesterase inhibitor approved for the treatment of mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease in adults. ZUNVEYL’s active metabolite is differentiated from donepezil and rivastigmine in that it binds neuronal nicotinic receptors, including the alpha-7 subtype, which has been studied in preclinical and clinical research. Benzgalantamine is also being developed in combination with memantine to treat moderate to severe Alzheimer’s dementia, and as a sublingual formulation for Cognitive Impairment with mTBI. title: Organization Feature Flags, OAuth2 Endpoint Auth & Billing
body_text: We shipped four features this week: organization-level feature flags, OAuth2 authentication for endpoints, a billing module, and better test infrastructure. Organization Feature Flags Feature flags used to be all-or-nothing across your entire Convoy instance. You can now manage feature flags at the organization level. Go to Settings → Early Adopter Features to enable features like OAuth2 token exchange and mTLS for your organization. Instance admins can also override feature flags for specific organizations from the admin panel. OAuth2 Authentication for Endpoints Some endpoints require OAuth2 authentication. Endpoints now support OAuth2 client credentials authentication with shared secret or JWT client assertion. Configure your OAuth2 settings in the endpoint form, and Convoy handles token exchange automatically. This feature requires an enterprise license and the OAuth Token Exchange early adopter feature flag enabled. Billing Module We added a billing module that calculates usage from your Convoy data. View monthly usage, manage subscriptions, handle invoices, and set up payment methods, all from the Convoy dashboard. Go to Settings → Usage and Billing to get started. This feature requires a billing module license and billing admin or organization admin role. E2E Test Infrastructure We rebuilt our end-to-end test infrastructure to make it more reliable and easier to maintain. Tests now use Docker containers for Redis and PostgreSQL, making them faster and more consistent across environments. Other Improvements UI refresh : We refreshed the dashboard UI with a cleaner design and better navigation Batch tracking : Track progress when retrying multiple event deliveries at once Admin UI : Instance admins can manage feature flags and circuit breaker configurations from a dedicated admin panel Job IDs : All queue jobs now use ULID-based job IDs for better tracking All features are available now. See the endpoints documentation for OAuth2 configuration details.

title: Strategies for migrating your life and annuity policy administration systems
summary: Migrating to modern systems is a business imperative, but not easily achieved. In this post, I’ll examine in more detail three strategies for successfully implementing these large, complex, and potentially risky programs.
body_text: Life and pensions (L&P) insurance carriers can face serious challenges when migrating their legacy policy administration systems (PAS) or when shifting blocks of business during acquisitions or other critical events. In our latest CGI Voice of Our Clients research, 77% of L&P executives say they are experiencing high to medium challenges with their legacy systems. Further, cloud migration and legacy modernization are executives’ top two cited IT priorities, respectively. Migrating to modern systems is a business imperative, but not easily achieved. While my previous blog— Life insurance policy administration system migrations - keys for staying on course —discussed some of the main complications that plague legacy PAS migrations, in this post, I’ll examine in more detail three strategies for successfully implementing these large, complex, and potentially risky programs. 1. Be realistic: Accurately assess scale and complexity Every PAS migration has several key elements that can create challenges: Multiple internal and external stakeholder groups Multiple workstreams, including sourcing legacy data and defining rules to correctly configure the target system (the platform your organization is migrating to) and ensure continuity for operations teams Complex inter-dependencies across operations, IT, and third-party vendors Significant budget/burn-rate issues requiring rapid decision-making and agility when implementation doesn’t go according to plan At the same time, a lack of experience in executing these projects can mean there is little in-house knowledge about how to structure and execute a program with such inter-dependencies. Given this complexity, we recommend that any organization undertaking a migration establish a strong program office that ensures dedicated representation from the following stakeholders: Business owners with expertise, including: Actuarial/product manufacturing Administration, with a focus in-force servicing complexities Distribution and claims, if impacted by the migration IT owners: Application and data services Integration services, including financial systems and document management Quality engineering Systems analysis/business analysis External vendors: Source PAS team, if maintained/operated by a third party Target PAS team, if maintained/operated by a third party Depending on how your company is organized and how many external partners you have and need, the above list can grow significantly. For example, when acquired books are involved, governance and coordination can rapidly become challenging. Failure to create a clear plan with defined ownership and dependencies often leads to on-the-fly changes in methodology or strategy, which can create a cascading set of challenges related to legacy data quality and policy valuation/balancing. 2. Think beyond data: Product analysis is key Migration is more than “just another data project.” While it’s true that data plays a significant role in any migration, business rules and related logic are of equally high importance. Because the source and target systems may have very different approaches in setting up products and administering policies, the mapping of data and rules across the systems can be complex. It’s important to focus on the insurance product complexities upfront by establishing joint product analysis teams early on, especially with products such as variable and indexed families. Examples of areas where common pitfalls occur include the following: Interest crediting rules and logic for investment-linked products Application of taxation rules Calculation logic and storage of various cash values (e.g., dynamically calculated cash surrender value versus stored cash surrender value) Interpretation of policy status (e.g., lapse or grace periods) between systems Finally, correctly configuring the target PAS as early as possible is crucial for conducting testing and reconciliation once test data is extracted from the legacy PAS. This often is a critical bottleneck with complex products. Although it can be tempting to shrink the testing and reconciliation window to accommodate delays in this configuration, doing so will lead to other issues, including short-changing operations testing and pushing defects into post go-live activities. 3. Attract and retain the right people For most carriers, migrating a PAS legacy system is a strategic initiative, but in-house teams may lack experience with execution. Success depends on bringing together the best talent from within the organization and from external partners, aligning talent with appropriate responsibilities, and ensuring the project is their primary focus during key periods. Following are some critical requirements based on CGI’s experience across multiple programs: Allocate experts with deep product/actuarial understanding : It can be challenging to recruit professionals with the experience needed to analyze and document products manufactured 30 years ago. However, finding these people and making these tasks a priority can help to mitigate downstream migration problems stemming from incorrectly configured products on the target system due to missed requirements with respect to both data and business rules. Engage operations experts who work with the legacy system and related products : Many arcane administration rules are not obvious, even after close analysis. People who work with the system daily have valuable knowledge that can positively shape the future state model. Including them at the table throughout the project to ensure all administrative nuances are accounted for will improve outcomes. It is crucial to include the operations experts throughout every phase of the project, from analysis and design to user acceptance testing (UAT). Focus on the IT team supporting the legacy PAS : On the IT side, the talent pool is often limited. Many legacy systems are either on limited support (users do the bare minimum and try to avoid breaking anything) or support has been outsourced. In many cases, there are vast areas of the system that have not been explored in many years, and documentation is usually incomplete or missing entirely. While finding the right people and ensuring their availability throughout the project is essential, it’s equally important to have a “plan B” to leverage source code analysis tools and techniques. At CGI, for example, we make extensive use of CAST tools to locate critical actuarial and administrative rules embedded in legacy code and stored procedures. Prioritizing the migration project means backfilling for key resources. For big projects with long timelines, it may make sense to hire contractors to support routine “run” operations, so that key resources do not get pulled into non-critical issues. External resources to consider include the following, Professional services from the target PAS : The vendor of the target system should offer professional services consultants, along with tools and methodologies unique to their platform. Carriers should include an analysis of the new platform vendor migration tools and processes in their due diligence during project planning. Specialized migration partners : Organizations like CGI have deep experience, critical methodology, and advanced tools that are crucial to a project’s success. In a legacy migration, specialized partners are the experts who can deliver results on time and on budget while effectively managing risk. I like to use the analogy of the home handyperson who can (eventually) figure out how to wire a three-way switch through trial and error. A licensed electrician, on the other hand, will get it right the first time. Your migration project is similar. You can protect your investment and get the desired results by including specialized partners at the beginning of your project. Program management : Smaller carriers may not have a core competency in legacy migration, especially for a large-scale initiative. External partners can provide additional capabilities focused on governance and methodology for stakeholder management and project execution. These offerings can save significant costs and reduce risk in the long run. The carrier should be honest in their assessment of internal program management capabilities when deciding whether to invest in external support. With a focus on setting up a strong program office and aligning the right talent before launching the project, a PAS migration project can be successful. In my next blog, I’ll explore a few of the surprising yet important details that can typically hinder a project, along with recommendations on how to address them. Contact me to explore how CGI can support your organization in its digital transformation journey.

title: Replit Alternatives: How to Pick the Right AI App Builder or Cloud IDE in 2026
summary: Key Takeaways Several strong alternatives to Replit exist for online coding and collaborative development in 2026, but the right choice depends on what you actually need. body_text: Key Takeaways Several strong alternatives to Replit exist for online coding and collaborative development in 2026, but the right choice depends on what you actually need. If you're searching for replit alternatives because of unpredictable billing, limited infrastructure control, or governance gaps, you're not alone. Teams across the spectrum-from solo developers to enterprise teams-are re-evaluating whether Replit still fits their development workflow. The best replit alternatives in 2026 fall into three categories you should understand before evaluating individual tools: AI app builders (Bolt.new, Lovable, Zite, Dyad) for fast prototyping and business apps, including mobile apps AI-assisted IDEs (Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot) for professional developers who want ai assisted coding without leaving their normal workflow Cloud IDEs (GitHub Codespaces, CodeSandbox, StackBlitz) for repo-first browser development with team collaboration Top alternatives for 2026 include GitHub Codespaces for full VS Code functionality, Cursor for ai features embedded in a local setup, and platforms like Bubble and Glide for no code platforms. The best choice depends on whether you need rapid AI prototyping or a robust environment for full-stack development. No single tool replaces Replit for everyone. Your replit alternative depends on team type, technical skill, data connectivity needs, governance requirements, and deployment constraints. Jet Admin is one option worth evaluating if your priority is building secure business apps and internal tools on top of existing data-but it's not a general-purpose code editor, and this article won't pretend otherwise. What Is Replit and Where It Starts Breaking Down in 2026 Replit launched in 2016 as a browser ide that made writing code as simple as opening a URL. Instant environments, support for dozens of languages, and a "press Run" experience made it a favorite for education, hackathons, and quick demos. Replit's Multiplayer mode allows four users to collaborate in real-time, and its more recent AI agent capabilities let users generate apps from natural language prompts. By 2026, Replit has evolved into a cloud development platform with agentic ai capabilities, a design canvas, and connectors. But that evolution has introduced friction that many replit alternatives now address: Pricing unpredictability : Replit uses effort-based billing for its ai agent. Small changes can trigger disproportionate costs. One student reported that Replit Agent cost them $85 in two days. Limited infrastructure control : Hard limits on CPU, RAM, concurrent apps, and network bandwidth constrain serious projects. Platform lock-in : Code export exists, but databases, auth, and hosting tie back to Replit, making migration to your own infrastructure painful. Sandbox constraints : For teams building production internal tools or full stack web apps, the sandbox model falls short. Replit is still valuable for learning and quick prototyping. But for teams that need repo-first development, predictable pricing, and enterprise governance, many replit alternatives now offer a better path. How to Evaluate Replit Alternatives: Criteria That Matter in 2026 Before diving into specific tools, use this framework to evaluate any replit alternative. Skim the criteria below, then use them as a checklist when testing each platform. Build speed and AI experience : How fast is the prompt-to-app cycle? AI-native tools allow applications to be generated from natural language prompts, but output quality varies. Look for reliable ai coding agents that handle multiple files, iterate on feedback, and don't break existing features when adding new ones. Data connectivity and internal tools suitability : Can the tool connect to your databases, rest api endpoints, spreadsheets like a Google Sheet, and SaaS tools? This matters most for business apps and internal tools that sit on top of existing data. Tools like n8n, a visual automation tool for connecting apps and APIs, can supplement platforms that lack deep integration out of the box (n8n cloud plans start at $24/month for 2,500 workflow executions). Extensibility and customization : Does the platform support extension support, code export, importing existing React code, or bringing your own stack? Can you mix generated UI with custom backend logic? Auth, permissions, and governance : Look for role based access control, SSO/SAML, audit logs, environment separation (dev/stage/prod), and access controls that meet compliance needs. Deployment and hosting : Does the tool handle deployment infrastructure, or do you deploy code to your own servers? Support for custom domains, CI/CD pipelines, and self hosting matters for production readiness. Pricing model and long-term cost : Subscription vs credit-based pricing, per-seat vs usage, hidden limits-these drive total cost. Understand whether you're paying for free usage up to a cap, or if costs scale unpredictably. Code ownership and portability : Do you own a github repo of readable code? How easy is migration? Version control integration is non-negotiable for serious work. Team collaboration and review workflows : Support for PRs, code review, pair programming, shared sandboxes, and review gates. Team management features separate prototyping tools from production-ready platforms. Replit Alternatives at a Glance: Comparison Table The table below summarizes the many replit alternatives covered in this article. Use it to quickly identify which category each tool belongs to and whether it fits your needs. Product Category Best For AI Role Code Ownership Production Readiness Typical Pricing Replit (baseline) Cloud IDE + AI agent Learning, prototyping Agentic (Agent, chat) Partial (export exists, services tied) Prototype / SMB Subscription + effort credits Cursor AI IDE (local) Professional developers Inline + chat + refactors Yes (your repo) Enterprise Paid plans start at $20/mo GitHub Codespaces Cloud IDE Repo-first teams Optional (Copilot add-on) Yes (GitHub repo) Enterprise Compute hours + storage Bolt.new AI app builder Fast prototypes, MVPs Prompt-to-app Yes (exportable) Prototype / SMB Free tier + paid credits Lovable AI app builder Design-led MVPs Prompt-to-app Yes (exportable) Prototype / SMB Free plan (30 credits); paid from $25/mo Bubble No-code app builder Custom web apps Workflow automation No (platform-bound) SMB production Paid plans from $69/mo Glide No-code app builder Spreadsheet-based apps Minimal Partial SMB production Free tier + paid plans CodeSandbox Cloud IDE Frontend prototyping Minimal Yes (repo-backed) Prototype Free + paid plans StackBlitz Cloud IDE Frontend / JS environments Minimal Yes (repo-backed) Prototype Free; Pro ~$18/yr Zite AI app builder Production business software Prompt-to-app Partial SMB / Enterprise Free plan (unlimited apps); paid from $19/mo Dyad AI app builder (local) Offline-first full-stack apps Local AI models Yes (open source) Prototype / SMB Free and open source Windsurf AI IDE Budget AI coding Agentic + inline Yes (your repo) SMB / Enterprise Generous free tiers Jet Admin Business app builder Internal tools on existing data Prompt-based + agents Yes (exportable) SMB / Enterprise Free plan + paid tiers Pricing and features change frequently. Verify current numbers on each vendor's site before making a decision. The categories above are meant to help you self-identify where you fit-not to rank tools against each other. Cursor: AI-First IDE for Developers Who Want Control Cursor integrates AI deeply into the coding workflow, functioning as a VS Code–style IDE installed locally. It's aimed at experienced developers who want strong ai assisted coding without leaving their normal workflow or giving up code ownership. Core strengths that make Cursor a standout replit alternative: Multi-file understanding : Cursor can reason across multiple files and large codebases, making architecture-aware refactors practical rather than theoretical. Model flexibility : Support for multiple LLM providers lets you choose the artificial intelligence model that fits your task and budget. Git-native : Standard git integration means your development workflow stays intact-PRs, branches, code review, and CI all work as expected. Collaboration : Cursor integrates AI into the coding workflow for enhanced collaboration, with team plans offering org-wide privacy, admin dashboards, and SAML/OIDC SSO. Cursor's paid plans start at $20/month for unlimited code completions, scaling to $60/month (Pro+) and $200/month (Ultra) for heavier usage. Team plans run approximately $40/user/month with enterprise options available. Cursor does require local setup and developer skills. It doesn't include turnkey hosting or one-click deployment. If you're a non-technical team looking for visual editing or a browser ide, Cursor isn't the right fit. Best for : Agencies, product engineering teams, and individual devs building production apps who want AI in their IDE instead of a hosted sandbox. Also worth noting: GitHub Copilot suggests code as you type in existing IDEs and costs $10/month for individuals, making it a lighter alternative if you prefer to stay in standard vs code. GitHub Codespaces: Cloud IDE for Repo-First Teams GitHub Codespaces is considered the most direct professional replacement for Replit. It provides a standardized cloud development environment for teams, offering full VS Code in the browser or desktop client, backed by dev containers. The experience shares Replit's "open a URL and code" simplicity, but environments are attached to real github repositories and standard Git workflows rather than a proprietary sandbox. You can import repositories, spin up cloud dev environments from any branch or PR, and get a reproducible setup defined by a devcontainer.json file. Key strengths: Reproducible environments : Dev containers eliminate "works on my machine" problems. Disposable environments mean onboarding a new developer takes minutes, not days. Deep GitHub integration : PRs, Actions, reviews, and git provider workflows all work natively. This supports a normal workflow for teams already invested in GitHub. Governance : Data residency is now available in public preview for Enterprise plans (US, EU, Australia), with policy controls, spending limits, and audit logging. AI layer : While Codespaces doesn't include a built-in prompt-to-app experience, you can layer in GitHub Copilot or other tools for ai capabilities. Limitations are real: pricing is based on compute time and file storage, which needs monitoring. There's no built-in visual editor or one-click app deployment-you need your own CI/CD and deployment infrastructure. Best for : Professional teams already on GitHub wanting browser-based development, predictable governance, and the ability to plug in AI without giving up repo ownership. Worth mentioning that Gitpod supports automated, reproducible development environments that work with Git repositories as well, offering an alternative cloud dev environment model. Bolt.new and Lovable: AI App Builders for Fast Prototypes Both Bolt.new and Lovable frequently appear in lists of best replit alternatives, but they serve a different purpose: rapid prototyping and vibe coding rather than long-term production development. Bolt.new Bolt generates full-stack applications from natural language prompts. Platforms like Bolt.new allow full-stack applications to be built simply by providing natural language prompts-typically using React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Node.js. The platform reports over 5.9 million apps created, with average build times under two minutes. Strengths include instant scaffolding, interactive prompting to add features, built-in database and auth, and hosting on bolt.host with custom domains on paid plans. It requires minimal setup-no local environment needed. Limitations surface when projects grow. Users report that adding new features can break previously working parts. Deployment infrastructure is lighter than full cloud IDEs, and teams often need to re-platform when moving to durable production environments. Running code in Bolt's sandbox works for demos but may not meet enterprise needs. Lovable Lovable generates full-stack web apps from simple prompts, with a design-led approach that emphasizes polished UIs and what the community calls vibe coding. With over 25 million projects created and SOC-2 Type II plus ISO 27001 certifications, Lovable has moved beyond pure prototyping. Lovable generates full-stack web apps from user prompts, and its free plan includes 30 credits per month. Lovable's paid plans start at $25/month for 100 credits. The platform supports over 20 connectors (Stripe, GitHub, Notion, Shopify, Slack) and offers code access for manual refinement. Limitations: backend complexity, advanced auth, or custom integrations may require significant manual work. When apps get complex, prompt drift becomes a real issue-fixes in one area break another. When to choose these over Replit : Pick them when design and prototype speed matter more than long-term governance or complex internal tools. For a real app headed to production, plan for eventual migration to a repo-first stack. Bubble and Glide: No-Code Replit Alternatives for Business Apps No-code platforms allow non-technical users to create applications, and both Bubble and Glide serve teams that need business apps and internal tools rather than raw code editors. Bubble Bubble is a no-code app builder for creating fully custom web applications. Its drag-and-drop UI, built-in database, workflow engine, and plugin ecosystem power complex SaaS-style apps without writing code. Bubble is a no-code platform for custom web applications that can handle surprisingly deep business logic. Strengths: depth of workflows, ability to handle complex business apps, built-in hosting and scaling. For teams that care more about functionality than code ownership, Bubble is a credible replit alternative that supports full stack web apps through visual editing. Limitations: code is not exported as a standard repo-teams accept platform lock-in. Performance and pricing scale together, which can surprise growing apps. Bubble's paid plans start at $69/month for web and mobile apps. There have also been security concerns when malicious actors exploited Bubble apps for phishing. Glide Glide turns spreadsheets into mobile and web-ready business apps. It's oriented around Google Sheets, Airtable, and similar data sources, making it excellent for spreadsheet-native operations teams. Glide turns spreadsheets into mobile and web apps with role based access and visibility rules, strong for SMB business apps. Strengths: quick internal tools, lightweight mobile apps, role-based visibility, and minimal coding required. If your data lives in a Google Sheet or Airtable, Glide can have an app running in hours. Limitations: Glide is best for data-centric apps and less suited to highly custom UIs or complex backend logic. The platform-first model means less flexibility than code-based alternatives. Guidance : Both are better replit alternatives for non-developers building internal tools or customer portals, but teams must weigh platform lock-in against speed. If you need unlimited apps and users on a free plan with a focus on production business software, also consider Zite, which specializes in building production business software from plain English prompts (Zite's paid plans start at $19/month for 100 credits). CodeSandbox and StackBlitz: Cloud IDEs for Frontend-Heavy Work These tools are closest to Replit's original browser-editor roots but optimized for modern frontend frameworks and collaborative prototyping in js environments. CodeSandbox CodeSandbox is an online cloud ide oriented around React, Vue, and similar stacks. It offers live sandboxes, sharing via URL, strong preview ergonomics, and real-time collaboration. CodeSandbox offers real-time collaboration features for web development, making it useful for design/development handoff, teaching, bug reproduction, and small front-end projects. It supports connecting to a github repo for more serious workflows and offers dev containers for environment reproducibility. Extension support for VS Code keybindings and extensions makes it feel familiar. Limitations: backends, databases, and long-lived production hosting are less central. Users often pair CodeSandbox with separate hosting and CI/CD for full products. StackBlitz StackBlitz runs instant in-browser environments using WebContainers for Node.js and front-end frameworks, delivering very fast boot times and good github integration . Its Pro plan costs approximately $18/year (annual) or $25/month, with team plans around $55/member/year. StackBlitz is a strong replit alternative for libraries and front-end teams who want "press play" code examples and unlimited browser-based sandboxes. It works well for documentation examples, reproducible sandboxes, and quick demos. Both tools share similar limitations: focus on front-end and prototyping, with limited support for complex multi-service backends, advanced governance, or enterprise deployment. Also worth noting: Glitch is beginner-friendly for web development and great for small Node.js projects, serving as another browser ide option for learners. For teams needing offline or local-first options, Dyad is an open-source AI app builder that runs locally. Dyad builds full-stack web apps using local AI models and allows local-first development with free local models-a genuinely different approach from cloud-dependent editors. Where Jet Admin Fits Among Replit Alternatives (and When It Doesn't) This section explains Jet Admin's positioning relative to Replit-style tools. It's written from Jet Admin's perspective, so take it as one data point in your evaluation rather than an objective ranking. Jet Admin is a platform focused on building secure business apps and internal tools on top of existing data. It connects to existing databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools, then generates the interface and application/backend logic needed to deploy the app to users. Unlike Replit, Jet Admin's core value is the application layer-UI, workflows, permissions-that sits above your existing systems. This makes Jet Admin a strong replit alternative in specific scenarios: Internal CRMs, admin panels, and operations dashboards where role based access control, audit logs, and data governance are requirements, not nice-to-haves. Teams that need code access without building everything from scratch: Jet Admin supports prompt-based app building, MCP/coding-agent workflows, and importing existing React code. Non- or semi-technical teams that need production-ready internal tools with governed access to company data and faster delivery than a generic IDE allows. Where Jet Admin is not the right fit: if you're building libraries, kernels, open-source projects, or generic consumer apps, a tool like Cursor or Codespaces is more appropriate. Jet Admin is not a developer's primary IDE, and it's not designed for low-level debugging tools or running code outside the context of business applications. If your priority is business apps, portals, or workflow tools, evaluate Jet Admin alongside Bubble, Glide, and Zite-focusing on data connectivity, permissions, and long-term maintenance rather than raw coding flexibility. Zite specializes in building production business software without coding and offers unlimited apps and users on its free plan, making it another relevant comparison point. Replit Alternatives for Different Team Types and Skills The right replit alternative depends on who's using it and what they need to build. Here's how to map tools to personas. Solo developers and small technical teams Emphasize Cursor, GitHub Codespaces, and StackBlitz. These offer repo-first workflows, strong ai assisted coding, and integration with existing toolchains. Windsurf offers generous free tiers and strong agents for budget AI options, making it another viable option for cost-conscious developers. Dyad allows local-first development for collaborative coding without internet, which suits developers with unreliable connectivity. Non-technical founders and small businesses Start with Bubble, Glide, Lovable, or Bolt.new. These app builder platforms turn natural language or spreadsheets into working business apps without heavy coding. Lovable and Bolt handle the visual editing and ai app generation; Bubble and Glide offer deeper no-code logic for ongoing apps. Product and operations teams needing internal tools Jet Admin, Glide, and Zite are purpose-built for this. Focus on role based access, auditability, and connecting to existing databases and SaaS systems. Team management, access controls, and deployment to private collections of users matter more here than raw coding power. Enterprises and regulated organizations GitHub Codespaces with policy controls, Cursor Enterprise, and StackBlitz self-hosted options provide the governance, SSO, audit logs, and data residency these teams require. AI agents should operate under permission and audit controls. Educators and learners Replit may still be fine here. CodeSandbox and StackBlitz also work well when code ownership and long-term maintainability are less critical. The free plan and free usage tiers on most tools make experimentation low-risk. Use whatever gets students running code fastest. Migration Checklist: Moving From Replit to a New Platform Moving away from Replit doesn't have to be a risky leap. Follow this step-by-step checklist to de-risk migration. Inventory phase Export all current Replit projects and document which ones use Replit-specific services (built-in DB, auth, file storage, hosting). Label each project: prototype, internal tool, or revenue-critical production system. List dependencies including databases, API keys, environment secrets, and any shared credentials. Target state decision Choose a target category for each project: AI IDE (Cursor, VS Code + Copilot), cloud ide (Codespaces, CodeSandbox), ai app builder (Bolt, Lovable, Zite), no-code platform (Bubble, Glide), or internal tools builder (Jet Admin). Avoid assuming one tool fits every use case. A team might use Cursor for their main product and Jet Admin for internal tools, for example. Repo-first transition Move code out of Replit into a git provider (GitHub, GitLab, etc.). Set up basic branch protections and PR workflows. Replace Replit's "push and it runs" model with CI checks and deploy code pipelines. Even a simple GitHub Actions workflow is an upgrade. Infrastructure separation Decide where to host apps: Vercel, AWS, a traditional VPS, or your platform's built-in hosting. Configure separate dev and prod environments. Do not tie deployment back to your new IDE. Keep development and deployment infrastructure independent. Data and auth migration Point apps to new databases or managed services. Migrate data safely with tested scripts. Replace any Replit-specific auth with standard identity providers (Auth0, Firebase Auth, etc.). If moving to an app builder, verify that role based access control and audit logs meet your compliance needs. Testing and rollback Define smoke tests for every migrated app. Include both functional and performance tests. Prepare rollback procedures so you can revert if migration introduces bugs. Communicate the plan to stakeholders and cut over gradually-avoid a "big bang" switch. How to Choose the Best Replit Alternative for Your Project in 2026 All the detail above boils down to a simple decision sequence: Define your primary outcome : Are you learning, prototyping, shipping production internal tools, or building consumer apps? Pick your category : AI app builder, cloud ide, AI IDE, or no-code platform. Shortlist 2–3 tools from that category and run a time-boxed trial. Practical filters to apply: Code ownership : If you need to deploy code to your own infrastructure or import repositories into your own stack, eliminate tools that don't support standard git integration. Technical comfort : Non-technical teams should lean toward no code platforms or ai app builders with visual editing. Developers should default to Cursor or Codespaces. Data sensitivity : If you're handling customer data, internal financials, or anything subject to regulation, filter for tools with audit logs, SSO, and data residency support. App type : Native mobile apps push you toward Glide or frameworks like React Native; web-only internal tools open up more options including Jet Admin and Bubble. Example decision patterns: Non-technical founder validating a SaaS idea : Start with Lovable or Bubble. If the idea works, plan a later migration to a code-based stack for scale. Engineering-led B2B team : Start directly with Cursor + Codespaces. Use other tools (like Google Docs for specs or n8n for automation) around a repo-first core. Operations team needing a dashboard this quarter : Evaluate Jet Admin, Glide, or Zite. Speed and governed data access matter more than coding flexibility here. Run each trial with a single representative project. Track build speed, friction, governance gaps, and how it integrates with multiple tasks in your existing workflow. Conclusion: Replit Alternatives and the Future of AI App Development The best replit alternative in 2026 depends on whether you prioritize speed, code ownership, internal tools, or governance-not on which tool has the flashiest ai agent demo. If you expect to grow beyond small prototypes or class projects, start repo-first and separate your development environments from hosting. This single decision prevents the platform lock-in that makes migration painful later. Map your needs against the evaluation criteria covered earlier: build speed, data connectivity, extensibility, auth and permissions, deployment, governance, pricing, and maintenance. No tool scores perfectly on all dimensions. The goal is to find the one that scores highest on the dimensions that matter most to your team. Your next step: shortlist 2–3 tools that match your use case, spin up a small test app on each, and compare the real-world experience against Replit. Pay attention not just to day-one speed but to long-term maintainability-how easy is it to update, debug, and hand off the project six months from now? If your priority is secure business apps and internal tools on top of existing data, include Jet Admin in that shortlist alongside more generic app builders and IDEs. FAQs About Replit Alternatives These questions tend to surface after teams start actively evaluating alternatives-not during initial research. Can I keep using Replit for learning while moving production work elsewhere? Many teams and individuals do exactly this: maintain Replit for tutorials, workshops, and experiments while shifting serious codebases to repo-first tools like Cursor or GitHub Codespaces. The split works well as long as you keep environments isolated. Avoid sharing credentials or environment secrets between your Replit sandbox and production systems. If students or junior developers are using Replit for learning while your team uses Codespaces for production, establish clear boundaries about which environments connect to which data. What's the safest option if I'm worried about code ownership? IDEs and cloud IDEs-Cursor, VS Code, Codespaces, CodeSandbox with repos-offer the strongest code ownership because everything lives in your github repo. You own the full source, version history, and deployment pipeline. No-code platforms and tightly coupled app builders (like Bubble) bind runtime and logic to the vendor, trading portability for speed. If code ownership is critical, keep core backend logic in exportable code and use private collections or repos to manage access. For teams that want open-source flexibility, Dyad allows local-first development with free local models and full code access. Are Replit alternatives better for internal tools than classic frameworks? Building internal tools directly in frameworks like React or Django offers maximum control but at higher engineering cost and slower iteration. Internal-tool-focused platforms-including Jet Admin, Bubble, and Glide-can significantly speed delivery if they meet your data, auth, and governance needs. The trade-off is flexibility: if your internal tool requires unusual integrations or highly custom backend logic, a framework gives you more room. Assess long-term integration requirements and auditability before committing. How do I combine an AI app builder with my existing CI/CD pipeline? Two common patterns work well. First, use the ai app builder only for initial scaffolding, then migrate the generated code to a github repo that feeds into your standard pipeline. Second, keep builder-driven code in a separate repo with automated syncing. Either way, ensure generated code is reviewable via PRs, add automated tests before exposing ai-generated changes to production, and never push directly from the builder into live environments without code review. This preserves your team's normal workflow while capturing the speed benefits of AI generation. Do any Replit alternatives support offline or low-connectivity development? Local IDEs like VS Code and Cursor are best when offline work is critical, since most cloud IDEs and ai app builders assume stable connectivity. Dyad allows local-first development for collaborative coding without internet, making it a unique option for remote or restricted environments. If you frequently work offline, favor local-first development with later synchronization to Git, using cloud tools sparingly for previews and team collaboration sessions.

title: Sequencing applications in adoptive cell therapy development
summary: Adoptive cell therapies are reshaping cancer care, driven by breakthroughs in gene editing, viral vector engineering, and next‑generation sequencing (NGS). Programs have expanded from hematologic cancers to solid tumors. However, the solid tumor microenvironment (TME) has emerged as a critical challenge to achieving therapeutic benefit, particularly when compared to hematologic cancers. Developers face demands for deeper product characterization, greater safety assurance, and more precise patient selection.
body_text: Image Maryland Franklin, PhD, is the vice president and enterprise head of cell and gene therapy (CGT) at Labcorp. With over 25 years of experience in drug development across a range of modalities spanning small molecules, antibodies, and CGTs, Maryland has partnered on multidisciplinary teams to deliver therapeutic candidates, and she has played a key role in bringing four drugs into Phase I oncology clinical trials. She leads a matrixed team of CGT experts driving strategic vision, thought leadership, and cross-sector global collaborations. Adoptive cell therapies are reshaping cancer care, driven by breakthroughs in gene editing, viral vector engineering, and next‑generation sequencing (NGS). Programs have expanded from hematologic cancers to solid tumors. However, the solid tumor microenvironment (TME) has emerged as a critical challenge to achieving therapeutic benefit, particularly when compared to hematologic cancers. Developers face demands for deeper product characterization, greater safety assurance, and more precise patient selection. Sequencing technologies provide insights to help overcome crucial obstacles and advance novel adoptive cell therapies with confidence. How are adoptive cell therapies currently used in clinical oncology practice and which patients are most likely to benefit? Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies are widely used, with seven FDA-approved therapeutics across hematologic malignancies as of May 2026. The field is also expanding into solid tumor indications with the first FDA approvals of a non-modified tumor‑Infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) product and a genetically engineered T-cell receptor (TCR) T-cell therapy in 2024. Numerous adoptive cell therapies are being evaluated in the clinical trial setting across solid tumor indications and target antigens. Clinical benefit, however, has been primarily limited to a subset of patients in hematologic malignancies. What barriers limit cell therapy adoption, and how can biomarker‑driven evaluation such as genomic profiling help mitigate these challenges? Key barriers to cell therapy adoption include safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and limitations related to clinical success in solid tumors. High-quality biomarker insights via measurements of cell persistence, potency, and on-target/off-tumor activity may help assess safety hurdles. Biomarker-driven evaluations like genomic profiling can provide a deeper understanding of the TME, tumor cell heterogeneity, and overall therapeutic response in patients. These insights can inform strategies to improve clinical success, for example, by modifying the TME to enhance CAR T-cell infiltration and cytotoxicity in solid tumors. How are biomarkers being applied during the development of cell therapy products? Biomarkers are foundational to adoptive cell therapy development. A multimodal biomarker strategy is essential, with platforms ranging from flow cytometry for real-time cellular tracking and phenotyping, functional (potency) assays to assess product quality, and genomic technologies (qPCR, dPCR, NGS) to evaluate vector copy number, persistence, off-target effects, and genomic safety. In earlier stages of development, strategies such as paired whole exome sequencing (WES) and whole transcriptome sequencing (WTS) yield deep insights into tumor biology and the TME. In clinical development, targeted assays may provide a cost-efficient method to track biomarkers of therapeutic response or resistance and cell persistence. For example, when we analyzed a cfDNA-derived genome instability number (GIN) in 12 relapsed B-cell lymphoma patients treated with autologous CAR T-cell therapy, we found correlations between the GIN levels and clinical and radiographic response, suggesting that cfDNA analysis may be useful in disease monitoring and relapse prediction. How do sequencing platforms support product quality, consistency, and safety? Adoptive cell therapy products are inherently variable due to factors including donor-to-donor differences and manufacturing complexities. Single-cell and bulk sequencing together with other multi-omics approaches are being implemented alongside traditional platforms to expand product characterization and enhance potency testing. Early application could improve donor or patient stratification, enable optimal candidate selection, and inform pre-conditioning strategies that would bolster T-cell fitness. Additionally, integrating omics approaches at the leukapheresis stage may meaningfully enhance manufacturing consistency and clinical efficacy. Sequencing is also central to evaluating safety during the development and manufacturing of adoptive cell therapies. Traditionally, it has been used to quantify vector copy number and map integration sites, which are key measures for assessing genotoxicity risk. Increasingly, sequencing also enables TCR repertoire profiling and precise genomic assessment of gene-edited products, providing critical insights into efficacy and product quality. What molecular data is being used to support regulatory approvals? There is growing use of comprehensive genomic and transcriptomic data to support regulatory guidance for product characterization and safety and potency assessment. Continued implementation of these strategies should improve safety, identity, purity, and potency, as well as overall product consistency and clinical readiness. Cell therapies are rapidly maturing treatment modalities, expanding beyond hematologic cancers into solid tumors. Labcorp provides integrated strategy and comprehensive biomarker testing solutions from preclinical research through clinical development, companion diagnostics, and commercialization. Explore Labcorp solutions to support your cell therapy development program. Biomarker Strategy Precision Oncology NGS Solutions Cell and Gene Therapy

title: Western Alliance Bank Named a Lyons Den Honoree by Arizona Bar Foundation
summary: Western Alliance Bank (NYSE: WAL) has been named a Lyons Den Awardee by the Arizona Bar Foundation for its work in supporting access to justice through the Interest on Lawyers’ Trust Accounts (IOLTA) program.
body_text: PHOENIX — Western Alliance Bank (NYSE: WAL) has been named a Lyons Den Awardee by the Arizona Bar Foundation for its work in supporting access to justice through the Interest on Lawyers’ Trust Accounts (IOLTA) program. The Lyons Den list represents banks that partner with the Arizona Bar Foundation in demonstrating strong, ongoing support of IOLTA. The award is named after George Lyons, an Arizona attorney who recognized the importance of strong collaboration between IOLTA institutions and the Foundation. Western Alliance Bank was honored at the Foundation’s Annual Awards luncheon at the State Bar’s convention in Tucson on June 25th, 2026, along with other legal leaders who are advancing access to justice. “At Western Alliance Bank, we are dedicated to improving access to justice for those in Arizona and around the country, and funds from IOLTA accounts are a powerful way to ensure justice is served,” said Paul Hawkins, managing director of Western Alliance Bank’s Juris Banking Group. “It is an honor to be named part of the Lyons Den.” Along with its work on IOLTA accounts, Western Alliance Bank works with nearly 200,000 Arizona students through Junior Achievement, helping them to gain a foundation in personal finance and career readiness. Western Alliance Bank’s access to justice work also includes Digital Disbursements, the proprietary technology platform that battles fraud and payment options for claimants in class action settlements, helping ensure that more money from these cases reaches claimants more efficiently. The Arizona Foundation for Legal Services & Education (Arizona Bar Foundation) provides technical and financial assistance to legal aid organizations, schools and community groups and promotes “Access to Justice for All Arizonans” by supporting law-related education and free legal services and by promoting statewide collaborative efforts. About Us Western Alliance Bank Western Alliance Bancorporation (NYSE: WAL) is one of the country’s top-performing banking companies and has ranked as a top U.S. bank by American Banker and Bank Director since 2016. Its primary subsidiary, Western Alliance Bank, is a leading national bank for business that puts customers first, delivering tailored business banking solutions and consumer products backed by outstanding, personalized service and specific expertise in more than 30 industries and sectors. With $90 billion in assets and offices nationwide, Western Alliance excels at helping businesses of all sizes capitalize on their opportunities to solve today and succeed tomorrow.

title: The 4 most reputable free ancestry search websites using DNA information
summary: Looking for DNA matches? Try FamilyTree DNA, MyHeritage, LivingDNA and GEDmatch.
body_text: How can I get DNA information on ancestry for free? While there is no free DNA test , several companies do allow you to get many useful features of their platform simply by uploading your previously acquired DNA data. No genealogist? No problem! The companies below will allow you to explore different aspects of your family story simply by setting up a free account and uploading a raw data file! ‍ Here’s some features with free access from various companies: Search for family members Conduct genealogical research Use search engine operations to find free family tree information Whether your relatives are Canadian, Indian, Jewish, British, Irish, Native American, or a mix of them all, there are some free tools below which can help you find vital information and records on free genealogy sites. Check it out! ‍ Family Tree DNA This company accepts tests from: 23andMe (Versions 3-5) AncestryDNA (Versions 1-2) MyHeritage ‍ ‍ ‍ FTDNA allows you to upload a file from any of the sources above to access their Family Finder Matrix. The Matrix is a program on their platform intended to find your closest relatives. This free tool may help you build your family tree, discover you family history, or conduct simple genealogy research. However, the free upload does NOT give you access to the full range of Family Finder features. ‍ For only $19 you can get access to these extra features which include the Chromosome Browser, myOrigins ethnicity estimate, and the ancientOrigins maternal and paternal haplotype test. You can check out their raw DNA data upload page here: https://www.familytreedna.com/autosomal-transfer ‍ MyHeritage This company accepts tests from: 23andMe LivingDNA AncestryDNA FamilyTreeDNA MyHeritage is one of the largest DNA genealogy sites around, competing with Ancestry.com and other testing companies. MyHeritage allows customers to upload data from any of the above companies for free, and free users can get access to living genetic matches to conduct a recent genealogy search. MyHeritage users are largely based in Europe. So, if you are looking for a British uncle, a cousin in Ireland, or a half brother in Germany, this is a good choice. With the free service you can also use the Chromosome Browser, and get an Ethnicity Estimate based on 42 different regions. ‍ Before the days of DNA testing, MyHeritage focused largely on creating software for genealogy resources such as family trees and a database of genealogical records. Records kept in the database include censuses, death records, military records, and passenger lists from European countries. To access these features, however, you must subscribe to the company’s service, starting at $139/year (the price jumps to starting at $189 in your second year of subscription). To learn more about uploading your data to MyHeritage, see the page below: https://blog.myheritage.com/2018/09/new-myheritage-supports-23andme-v5-and-living-dna-uploads/ ‍ ‍ LivingDNA This company accepts tests from: AncestryDNA 23andMe MyHeritage FamilyTreeDNA Gene by Gene Geno 2.0 LivingDNA is a genetic genealogy company based mainly in the United Kingdom. Using raw data files from any of the companies above, you can upload your sample to the LivingDNA platform. With a free account you will be able to access the DNA Matching portal, which will give you access to any DNA matches present within the LivingDNA database. ‍ However, with a free upload users will NOT receive the detailed ancestry reports provided to paying consumers. LivingDNA offers autosomal, mtDNA, and Y DNA tests which can analyze everything from your recent ancestry to deep ancestral information such as your DNA haplogroup. For this, you will have to purchase a DNA test kit. To see more information on uploading to LivingDNA, see the following page: https://support.livingdna.com/hc/en-us/articles/360012509652-What-format-does-my-file-need-to-be-in-to-successfully-upload- ‍ ‍ GEDmatch This company accepts tests from: 23andMe FamilyTreeDNA AncestryDNA Most other companies The GEDmatch platform is not nearly as user-friendly as other sites. However, it can be far more powerful if you learn how to use it. A lot of genealogy enthusiasts upload to GEDmatch to look within its expanded pool of people for more DNA matches that may not exist in their original testing company’s database; the ability to transcend the barriers between many testing companies is a clear advantage of the GEDmatch platform. ‍ Plus, many of the most powerful tools for genealogy research are completely free on GEDmatch. These tools include an admixture analysis (aka ethnicity estimate), autosomal DNA comparison with matches, X-DNA comparison, and even tools to compare GEDCOM family tree files created by other sites. This tool could be an extremely powerful free ancestry DNA test if it is used properly. ‍ For a donation of $10/month, the site will also give you access to a number of “Tier 1” tools. These include an enhanced DNA comparison, the ability to separate your maternal and paternal autosomal DNA, and the ability to estimate a deceased person’s DNA using the Lazarus tool. If you’re interested in learning more in specific detail about how to use GEDmatch, see our blog post on this topic . ‍ ‍ Other Ancestry Options Many genealogical/DNA sites are focused on European ancestry. However, if you are American or your family is from Canada, you may have better luck finding genealogical records (historical records, census records, national archives) from North America by using Ancestry.com . However, it is not a free genealogy website, and the cost of accessing their U.S. records starts at $19.99/month. ‍ Besides the free sites listed above, there are a number of other sites which show you many other aspects related to your DNA, such as information about your metabolism, personality, intelligence, physical traits, and various health reports. Many of these sites are also free. You can check a compiled list of DNA upload sites here . How to Check My Ancestry ‍ There are several ways to check your ancestry using DNA analysis. One of the most popular methods is to take a DNA test. These tests typically involve collecting a sample of your DNA, often through a saliva sample, and sending it to a testing company. The company will then analyze your DNA and provide you with a report that includes information about your ancestry and can also include information about your genetic health, inherited traits, and potential family matches. ‍ There are many companies that offer DNA testing for ancestry purposes, including Ancestry DNA, 23andMe, MyHeritage, and LivingDNA, among others. Each company has its own strengths and weaknesses, so it's important to do some research and read reviews to find the best option for you. ‍ Ancestry DNA Review ‍ Ancestry DNA is a popular DNA testing service that provides customers with insights into their family history and genetic makeup. With a database of over 18 million individuals, Ancestry DNA has become one of the most comprehensive ancestry services on the market. One of the standout features of Ancestry DNA is the company's large database of user profiles. With so many users, Ancestry DNA can provide customers with a wealth of information. ‍ Ancestry DNA does not offer free DNA testing, but they sometimes offer discounts and special offers. The regular price for Ancestry DNA testing is $99. Ancestry DNA also offers a subscription service that provides access to genealogical records and additional features, but this is a separate service from DNA testing and requires a monthly or yearly fee. ‍ Summary of Free Ethnicity Tests ‍ There is no free DNA test available, but some companies allow you to upload previously acquired raw DNA data and access many useful features of their platform for free. While some DNA testing companies may occasionally offer discounts or promotions on their ethnicity testing services, there are no DNA testing companies that offer a completely free ethnicity test. ‍ The cost of developing and processing the test is generally high, which makes it difficult for companies to offer the service for free. However, some companies may offer free DNA uploads or other free features related to DNA testing, but these may not be related specifically to ethnicity testing. The 4 most reputable ancestry testing companies that offer free services are Family Tree DNA, MyHeritage, LivingDNA, and GEDMatch. ‍ Family Tree DNA allows you to upload a raw data file and use their Family Finder Matrix to find your closest relatives for free. ‍ MyHeritage is one of the largest DNA genealogy sites, and free users can get access to living genetic matches. ‍ LivingDNA accepts raw data from various DNA testing companies, and offers DNA matching for free. ‍ GEDmatch is another platform that accepts DNA data from multiple companies and offers powerful genealogy research tools, including free admixture analysis and autosomal DNA comparison with matches. ‍ Ultimately, the best way to check your ancestry through DNA analysis will depend on your personal preferences, goals, and budget. A DNA test can be a great starting point, but it's also worth exploring other resources to get a more complete picture of your genetic heritage. If you have raw DNA data and would like to explore new aspects of your genetic history, get started today for FREE with Genomelink. ‍ To find out more DNA upload sites, check out our article "The Best DNA Upload Sites"

title: Use Cases for Production AI Agent Infrastructure & AURA | Mezmo
summary: Explore six production use cases for AURA, Mezmo's open-source, MCP-native agent harness, from drop-in chat agents to runbook-grounded RCA.
body_text: How platform and SRE teams are using Mezmo's open-core agent framework — with any LLM, any tools, any observability backend. By the Mezmo Engineering Team • March 2026 • 8 min read When we open-sourced AURA under the Apache 2.0 license, we made a deliberate choice: the agent infrastructure that powers Mezmo's own agentic SRE capabilities should be available to every team building production AI workflows. Not a stripped-down SDK. Not a managed-only service. The same framework we run internally, released as an open-core project where Mezmo is the primary contributor and steward. AURA (now available at https://github.com/mezmo/aura ) is a production-ready framework for composing AI agents from declarative TOML configuration. It is built in Rust, with MCP tool integration, vector search, and an OpenAI-compatible streaming API. It is intentionally agnostic: you choose your LLM provider, you connect your tools through MCP, and your telemetry goes wherever you send it via OpenTelemetry. This post walks through concrete use cases where AURA is already delivering value. Each scenario includes the architectural pattern, the relevant AURA configuration, and the operational outcome so you can evaluate whether this fits your own stack. Use case 1: Drop-in AI agent for existing chat UIs Your team has already standardized on a chat interface like LibreChat, OpenWebUI, or a custom frontend that speaks the OpenAI protocol. You want to add an AI agent that can call operational tools (query logs, check dashboards, pull runbooks), but you don't want to rewrite your frontend or build custom API integrations. With AURA AURA exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint with streaming SSE support. Point your existing frontend at AURA's address and it works immediately, with no protocol translation and no adapter code. Behind that endpoint, AURA routes requests to whichever LLM provider you've configured (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, or Ollama for local models) and dynamically discovers MCP tools at runtime. Beyond tool connectivity, AURA also provides native vector search support for incorporating company knowledge bases and runbooks directly into your agent's context. Vector stores are configured in your TOML alongside everything else, with Qdrant as the currently supported external provider. This means your chat agent doesn't just call tools — it can query your team's operational documentation to ground its responses in institutional knowledge. Configuration snapshot ‍ The key here is that AURA plugs into your existing ecosystem rather than replacing it. Your team keeps the chat UI they already know. And while AURA does take over the MCP tool layer, that's intentional: instead of managing tool connections scattered across individual agents, you configure them once in AURA and every agent benefits. Mezmo, PagerDuty, your own internal services are all registered in one place, with one schema, and AURA handles the orchestration, translation, and vector search from there. Any service your agent needs to interact with must expose an MCP endpoint. AURA connects to tools through MCP — that is the integration contract. If a tool has an MCP server, AURA can discover and invoke it. If it doesn't, that's the piece you'd need to build or find. Use case 2: Runbook-grounded incident response agent When an incident fires at 3 AM, the on-call engineer doesn't need a chatbot that guesses. They need an agent that references the team's actual runbooks, understands the service topology, and provides grounded recommendations rather than hallucinated ones. With AURA AURA's vector search is ready to go out of the box. We intentionally moved away from traditional RAG (where retrieved chunks are injected into the context window upfront) in favor of a query-based approach. The agent queries vector stores on demand during a conversation, pulling in only the information relevant to the current question. This avoids pre-polluting the context window with documents that may not be relevant, which in our experience hurt more than it helped outside of pure knowledge base scenarios. Currently, Qdrant is the supported external vector store. You configure your collections directly in TOML, and each collection gets a context_prefix that gives the LLM a concise description of what the collection contains and when to search it. Think of it as a label — something like "Mezmo Operations Manual" or "Payment Service Architecture" — that tells the model which knowledge base is relevant for a given question. Configuration snapshot The query-based approach keeps the agent's context window clean. Instead of stuffing every potentially relevant document into the prompt before the conversation starts, the agent searches the vector store as needed and pulls in targeted results. When the agent tells your on-call engineer to restart a specific service, the engineer can see that the recommendation was informed by the collection labeled "Company incident response runbooks" rather than by the model's general training data. This is the difference between an agent your team trusts and one they ignore. Use case 3: Flexible LLM provider selection Different teams, different use cases, and different cost profiles call for different models. Maybe your incident response agents need a frontier model on Anthropic, but your log summarization workflow runs fine on a local open-source model. Or maybe you want to run the same model through AWS Bedrock instead of directly through the provider for compliance reasons. You need the flexibility to make these choices in configuration, not in code. With AURA AURA supports five LLM providers out of the box: OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Gemini, and Ollama. Changing providers is a configuration change, not a code change. That said, it's worth being honest about what "configuration change" means in practice. Swapping from Anthropic direct to Anthropic via Bedrock is genuinely straightforward since you're running the same model family. Switching between fundamentally different model families (say, from Claude to Gemini) will often require prompt adjustments as well, because models don't all respond to the same prompting patterns in the same way. Where this flexibility really shines is with models available across multiple providers. Claude models, for example, can be accessed through both Anthropic's API and AWS Bedrock. AURA lets you make that routing decision in config based on your compliance, latency, or cost requirements — without touching any application logic. Because AURA automatically sanitizes MCP tool schemas to conform to each provider's function-calling requirements (handling quirks like anyOf wrappers, missing types, and optional parameter formats), your tool integrations remain stable across provider changes. The schema translation happens at discovery time, so the tools themselves don't need to know which LLM is on the other end. Open-source model support We actively test AURA against leading open-source models using platforms like Ollama (via the Ollama provider) and llama.cpp (via the OpenAI provider). Local quantized models can sometimes emit malformed structured outputs, which breaks tool-calling workflows. AURA includes fallback tool-call parsing that works around these known issues so open-source models remain viable in production. Use case 4: Authorization delegation to downstream tools Your agent calls MCP tools that require authentication, and the credentials need to come from the original user's request — not from a hardcoded service account. Different users should only be able to access what their own tokens authorize. You need the auth context to flow through AURA and into the downstream tool calls cleanly. With AURA AURA's headers_from_request configuration forwards incoming HTTP headers to downstream MCP servers on a per-request basis. This means the authentication token from the original user request flows through to every tool call, enabling per-tenant isolation without any custom middleware. Configuration snapshot The mapping is explicit: each key is the header name from the inbound request, and each value is the header name to send to the MCP server. In the example above, both Authorization and X-Tenant-ID headers are propagated to the MCP server, which can then enforce access control per customer. This keeps AURA stateless. It doesn't manage sessions, store tokens, or make authorization decisions. It routes the caller's credentials to the tools and lets each service enforce its own policies. For platform teams operating AURA as shared infrastructure, this is the cleanest pattern: the agent layer handles orchestration, and auth stays with the services that own the data. Use case 5: Understand what your agent is doing and why You're running AI in production and struggling to understand why it behaves a certain way. Standard application tracing tells you that an HTTP request took 4 seconds, but it doesn't tell you which tools the agent called, what context was retrieved from the vector store, how long the LLM took to respond, or what reasoning led to the final output. With AURA AURA ships with OpenTelemetry support enabled by default, and we chose the OpenInference semantic conventions ( llm.* , tool.* , input.* , output.* ) for our span attributes. We went with OpenInference because it was purpose-built for AI observability. It captures the semantics that matter for debugging agent behavior: LLM invocations, tool calls, retrieval operations, and the relationships between them. This means AURA traces are natively compatible with Arize Phoenix and any other OpenInference-aware observability tool — but they also export cleanly to any OTLP-compatible backend. Set your OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT environment variable and traces flow to Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, Mezmo, or wherever your team already looks. Backend agnostic: your AI observability data goes wherever your existing telemetry goes. No vendor lock-in on the tracing side either. Use case 6: Embedding AURA's core in your own Rust application You don't want a standalone HTTP server. You want to embed AI agent capabilities directly into your own Rust service, calling the agent builder programmatically, customizing the tool orchestration logic, and integrating at the library level. With AURA AURA is not a monolith. It's structured as three independent Rust crates with clear separation of concerns: aura — The core agent builder library. Runtime agent composition, MCP integration, tool orchestration, and vector workflows. No config file dependencies. aura-config — Typed TOML parsing and validation. Can be extended to support JSON, YAML, or any other format. aura-web-server — The OpenAI-compatible REST/SSE serving layer. Use it as-is or replace it with your own HTTP layer. If you only need the agent builder, depend on the aura crate directly. You get MCP tool discovery, schema sanitization, vector search, and multi-provider LLM support without pulling in any web server or config-file machinery. Mezmo's open-core model: what it means in practice AURA is not a side project or a marketing exercise. It is the agent infrastructure layer that powers Mezmo's own Agentic SRE product. The same codebase that runs in our production clusters is what ships on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. What this means concretely: Mezmo is the primary contributor. We maintain the project, merge PRs, publish releases, and run the CI pipeline. The repo has a CLA, a code of conduct, and contributing guidelines because we take community participation seriously. Production-hardened by default. Features like graceful shutdown, streaming backpressure controls, request cancellation, and timeout configuration exist because Mezmo needs them in production. You get those same guarantees. No vendor lock-in by design. AURA doesn't require Mezmo as a backend. Use it with any compatible LLM provider, any MCP servers (over HTTP), and any OTLP-compatible observability platform. If you're already a Mezmo customer, AURA integrates natively with our telemetry pipeline and MCP server. If you're not, it integrates just as cleanly with whatever you do run. The roadmap is visible.
